transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, honestly, doctor, I don't even know where to begin. I guess... well, I'm just completely falling apart. It really all started when those foreclosure notices started coming in the mail. I mean, they just keep arriving, and every time I see one, or even think about the mail, my stomach just drops. It’s like this heavy, sick feeling that I can’t shake. 

Ever since those letters started showing up, I just feel like I’m coming apart at the seams. I’m a heavy equipment mechanic, right? I work on massive diesel rigs, excavators, loaders... it’s a tough environment, you gotta be thick-skinned and focused. But lately? I’m sitting out in my pickup in the shop parking lot before my shift, just bawling my eyes out. Just crying over the steering wheel, trying to get it together for twenty minutes before I finally force myself to clock in. 

And if my cell phone rings? I practically jump out of my skin. I just flinch and my heart starts pounding because I'm terrified it's the bank calling again. And it’s spilling over into my work, which is what really scares me. I’m snapping at the young apprentices over every little thing—if they hand me a 3/8ths instead of a half-inch drive, I just bite their heads off, which isn't fair to them at all. And worse, I'm making mistakes. Stupid, careless mistakes in the repair bay. Things I have never, ever made in my entire career turning wrenches, like forgetting to double-check a high-pressure fitting. I just... I can't keep it together anymore, and I don't know how to fix it.
Have you ever had a sudden feeling of intense fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes?

Well, no, I wouldn't say it's a sudden thing that just peaks out of nowhere, if that's what you mean. It's not like a lightning bolt of fear. It’s... well, it’s more like this constant, heavy, grinding dread that just never really leaves me alone. 

Like I mentioned with the cell phone ringing—sure, I jump, and my heart does a little tap dance because I'm scared it's a debt collector, but it doesn't build up into this huge, overwhelming peak of terror for minutes on end. It’s just a quick jolt, and then I'm right back to that same low, sick feeling in my gut that I've had all day. I mean, from the second my alarm goes off at 4:30 in the morning and I'm lacing up my steel-toes, I'm already chewing on it. I'm thinking about the mortgage, I'm wondering where in the world I'm going to put all my heavy Snap-on toolboxes if the bank actually takes the house, how I'm going to explain it to people... 

So, no, it's not a sudden attack of fear that comes and goes. It's just always, always there. It's just sitting right on my chest, weighing me down while I'm trying to wrench on these rigs and keep my head straight for ten hours a day.
Have you been avoiding social situations or gatherings because of your current state?

Oh, absolutely. I mean, it's just completely taken over everything. It’s funny you ask that, because I used to be so involved in things, you know? Like, I’ve always been the type to keep busy. But now? I just... I can't. 

For instance, at work—and this is the part that really stings—they actually took me out of the high-risk repair bay. My supervisor, Dave, pulled me aside last Tuesday... or maybe it was Wednesday? Anyway, he said I just seemed too distracted to be working under suspended loads or dealing with the high-pressure hydraulics right now, which, honestly, he's not wrong about, considering the mistakes I mentioned earlier. But it's humiliating. I'm practically doing lube-tech work now, sweeping up and organizing parts bins. 

And outside of the shop? Forget about it. I used to volunteer at my church every other Sunday, helping run the food pantry. I haven't been in a month. I just can't face those people, you know? They’re all so nice and they always ask how I’m doing, and I know if I try to answer, I’ll just start crying right there in the fellowship hall. I also stopped going to my Wednesday night Zumba fitness classes. I used to love those—it was a great way to sweat out the grease and grime from the week, but now I just drive straight home, lock the door, and stare at the wall. 

Even my truck club... I have this group of friends, we all have classic Chevy C10s, and we usually do a cruise-in at the Sonic over on Route 9 every first Saturday of the month. We pop the hoods, talk shop, grab a burger... I haven't shown my face there since the first foreclosure notice arrived. I just keep making up excuses. I tell them I'm waiting on parts, or I have a migraine, but the truth is, I just can't stomach the idea of standing around making small talk and pretending everything is fine when I feel like my whole life is literally being repossessed. I just don't want to be around anyone. It's too exhausting to pretend.
Do you feel anxious when you're alone with your thoughts?

Oh, well, that's... yeah, that's really when it gets the worst, to be honest. When I'm just sitting there by myself. I mean, at work, even though I'm just organizing parts bins and sweeping up right now, at least my hands are moving, you know? At least I have to focus on putting the 10-millimeter sockets in the right drawer and not mixing up the O-rings. But when I go home... it's just me. I live alone, well, just me and my cat, Buster, but he's not exactly a great conversationalist. 

So I get home, I lock the door, and the house is just so quiet. And that's when my brain just starts going a million miles an hour. I'll sit down on the couch—I don't even turn the TV on anymore, I just sit there—and the thoughts just start piling up on top of each other. I start thinking about the bank, and then I think about the letters, and then I start picturing them coming to change the locks. I imagine where I'm going to sleep. I think about my tools, my big roll-cab toolbox that I've been paying off for five years... how am I going to move it? Where does it go if I don't have a garage? 

It just spirals. It's like a snowball rolling downhill, just getting bigger and heavier. And I sit there and my chest gets tight, and my stomach is just tied in these awful knots, and I can't stop it. I try to tell myself to just breathe, or to go make some tea or something, but I just end up frozen there on the couch for hours, just trapped in my own head with all these terrible scenarios playing out like a movie I can't turn off. So, yeah, being alone with my thoughts... it's honestly the most agonizing part of my entire day. I almost dread going home because I know what's waiting for me in the quiet.
Have you been experiencing any changes in your appetite or sleep patterns lately?

Well, as far as changes in my appetite or sleep... I mean, I guess I haven't really noticed anything major with either of those. It's funny, because you'd think with all this stress, I'd be stress-eating or not sleeping a wink, but... I don't know, my eating habits seem pretty much the same. I still pack my lunch for work every day—usually just a turkey sandwich, maybe some pretzels, an apple if I remember to grab one from the bowl on the counter. And for dinner, well, I still manage to throw something together, even if it's just heating up a can of soup or making some mac and cheese. I don't really have the energy to cook a big meal, but I'm still eating my normal amounts, I suppose. I haven't lost or gained any weight that I can tell. My work pants still fit the same, anyway.

And sleep... well, I still go to bed around 9:30, like I always do, because my alarm goes off at 4:30. I mean, I lay there for a bit with all those thoughts I was just telling you about, but I eventually drift off. I don't think I'm waking up in the middle of the night any more than usual. Buster sometimes jumps on the bed and wakes me up, but that's been happening for years. So, yeah, I wouldn't say my sleep or my appetite have really changed. It's just... everything else that feels like it's falling apart.
Do you often feel guilty or worthless about your current situation?

Guilty? Worthless? Oh, God, yes. All the time. I mean, it's just this constant, heavy feeling sitting right on my chest. It's like... how did I let this happen, you know? I'm 47 years old. I've been working since I was 16. I've been turning wrenches and busting my knuckles for decades, and for what? To lose my house? To be sweeping floors at the shop because I can't be trusted around a hydraulic lift anymore? 

I just keep running it over and over in my head. Like, if I had just picked up more overtime last year, or if I hadn't bought that new snap-on diagnostic scanner... which, by the way, I needed for the newer diesel engines, but still, it was expensive. I keep thinking I should have been smarter. I should have seen this coming. I feel so incredibly stupid. And worthless? Yeah, absolutely. When Dave pulled me off the high-risk bay... I mean, I know he was doing it for safety, I know I was messing up, but it just completely broke me. My job, being a mechanic, fixing things that are broken... that's who I am. That's my identity. If I can't even do that right, if I can't even keep a roof over my own head, then what good am I? 

I look at my friends in the truck club, and they're all doing fine. They're upgrading their suspensions, putting new crate motors in their C10s, and I'm just... I'm a complete failure. I feel like I've let myself down, I've let my parents down—God rest their souls, they'd be so ashamed if they saw me right now, facing foreclosure. It's just this overwhelming sense of guilt that I ruined my own life, and I don't even know how to fix it. I can fix a blown transmission, but I can't fix this, and it makes me feel like I'm just completely useless.
Do you feel anxious most of the time, even when there's no immediate threat or stressor?

Anxious most of the time? Even when nothing is happening? Um... no, I wouldn't really say that. I mean, don't get me wrong, I'm a mess about the house and the bank and work, but... it's not like I'm just sitting around terrified of, I don't know, the sky falling or something. If there's no reason to be anxious right in front of me, or if my brain isn't actively chewing on the foreclosure, I can actually feel somewhat normal for a minute. 

Like yesterday, for example. I was at the shop, and Dave had me reorganizing the entire back stockroom. It's tedious work, just counting boxes of air filters and matching part numbers to the inventory sheet on the clipboard, but for about two solid hours, I was just... doing it. I wasn't panicked. My heart wasn't racing. I was just looking at a box that said "Fleetguard FS1000" and making sure it went in the right bin. I wasn't worried about anything else in the world except those filters. And sometimes, if I'm driving home and a really good song comes on the radio—like old Bob Seger or something—I can just listen to the music and watch the road, and I don't feel that tight knot in my stomach. 

So, no, it's not this constant, free-floating panic all day long. It's very specifically tied to the mess I'm in. When the mail comes, or when I look at my toolbox, or when I'm alone in the quiet like I said before... that's when it hits me like a ton of bricks. But if I can manage to distract myself, or if there's literally nothing going on to trigger it, I don't feel that anxiousness. It's really just the reality of my situation that's causing it, not some random fear out of nowhere. If I could just fix the money issue, I know I'd be perfectly fine.
Do you worry about things other than your financial situation and work?

Worry about other things? Like... besides the money and the shop? Um... no, not really. I mean, I guess it's hard to even find the brain space to worry about anything else right now. It's like my head is just a one-track mind, and that track is heading straight for a cliff. 

I don't really worry about my health or anything like that. I mean, I'm 47, I've got a few aches and pains from being bent over engine bays all day, but nothing that keeps me up at night. I don't worry about getting sick, or... I don't know, world politics or whatever people watch on the news. I used to care a bit more about that stuff, maybe watch the evening broadcast while I ate my dinner, but lately, I just leave the TV off. I can't be bothered to care about what's happening in Washington when I'm about to lose my own living room, you know?

And I don't really worry about my friends or family. Like I said, my parents passed away a few years back, so I don't have to worry about taking care of them as they get older, which is a small mercy, I suppose. And my friends in the truck club, they're all doing fine. Better than fine, actually. They've got their lives together. So I don't fret over them. Really, it's just this one massive, overwhelming thing. The foreclosure, the bank, Dave pulling me off the floor... it just consumes everything. It's like a black hole right in the middle of my life, sucking all my attention and energy into it. So, yeah, if you take away the financial mess and the work stuff, I don't think I'd have a single care in the world. But unfortunately, I can't just take it away, can I? It's right there, all the time.
Do you feel sad or depressed most of the time?

Sad? Depressed? I mean... I don't think I'd use those words. When I think of somebody who's depressed, I picture someone who just lays in bed all day in the dark, crying, and can't even, you know, find the will to put their boots on. That's not me at all. 

I'm up at 5:30 every single morning, just like I have been for twenty-odd years. I make my coffee—black, same as always—I lace up my steel-toes, and I drive my truck down to the shop. I'm not sitting around weeping in the breakroom. It's not... it's not sadness, really. Like, I know what sadness feels like. When my old yellow lab, Buster, passed away about five years ago? Now that was sadness. I cried for a week straight. I couldn't even look at his empty leash hanging by the door without losing it. 

This isn't that. This is more like... this intense, boiling frustration. Like I'm backed into a corner and I'm trying to loosen a rusted bolt but I don't have the right size breaker bar, and I'm just stripping the threads. I'm just constantly kicking myself. Like yesterday, Dave asked me in passing how I was holding up with the bank stuff, and I didn't feel sad, I just felt this hot flash of embarrassment and anger. I just wanted to punch the cinderblock wall. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm walking around sad most of the time. I'm just completely drained and furious that I let my life get to this point where the bank is sending me certified letters in the mail every other week. If I were genuinely depressed, I probably wouldn't even care about the house anymore, right? I'd just give up. But I do care. I care so much it's absolutely eating me alive. I want my bay back, I want my life back, and I'm just mad that I screwed it all up. But sad? No, I really don't think that's the right word for it.
Do you think you would feel anxious if you weren't dealing with the foreclosure and work issues?

Oh, absolutely not. If you took away the bank and the shop mess, I'd be my old self in a heartbeat. I can trace it exactly back to when those foreclosure notices started showing up in the mail. Before that, I was rock solid. But ever since that first certified letter arrived... I just feel like I’m completely coming apart at the seams. It's like my whole system is just overloaded and I can't handle basic things anymore. 

Take my mornings, for instance. I used to just grab my coffee, listen to the morning show on the radio, and head in, ready to tackle a transmission rebuild or whatever was on the board. Now? I pull into the shop parking lot, sit in my truck with the engine running, and I just start crying. I don't even want to, the tears just come out of nowhere. I have to sit there wiping my eyes with a fast-food napkin for ten minutes before I can even pull myself together enough to walk through the bay doors. 

And my nerves are just completely shot all day long. Every single time the phone rings—whether it's my cell buzzing in my pocket or the loud ringer on the landline over by the parts desk—I literally jump. My shoulders hit my ears because I'm terrified it's a debt collector calling again, or Dave calling me into the front office to tell me he's letting me go completely. 

It's even bleeding into how I treat people, which I really hate. We have these two new apprentices at the shop, young kids, maybe 19 or 20, fresh out of diesel tech school. Normally I have a lot of patience for the greenhorns, you know? I like showing them the right way to bleed a brake line on a Peterbilt or how to properly pack a bearing. But lately? I'm snapping at them over the absolute smallest things. Like, if one of them hands me a 9/16 wrench when I clearly asked for a half-inch, I just bite their head off. I yelled at one of the kids so loud on Tuesday that the air compressors were running and people still turned around to look. 

But the worst part... the absolute worst part, and the thing that really scares me, is that I'm making stupid mistakes in the repair bay. Mistakes I never, ever would have made before all this started. I've been turning wrenches for over twenty years! But just last week, I completely forgot to torque the lug nuts on a dual-wheel axle. I just... I got distracted thinking about the mortgage, and I walked right past it. Thank God Dave was doing a final walk-around and caught it before the rig rolled out, because if that wheel had come off on the highway, it could have killed somebody. I felt sick to my stomach for two days over it. So, yeah, if the foreclosure and the work stuff were gone, none of this would be happening. I wouldn't be acting like this. It's 100 percent because of the mess I'm in.
Do you think your anxiety would decrease significantly if your financial and work situation were to improve?

Oh, God, yes. Yes, I really do. If I could just wake up tomorrow and the bank called to say, "Hey, we worked it out, your house is safe," or if Dave came up to me and said, "You're back on the heavy repairs full-time, don't worry about it," I swear to you, this whole nightmare in my head would just evaporate. I’d be completely back to normal in a heartbeat. 

But... well, the thing is, I can't really prove that yet, because the foreclosure process still isn’t resolved. Not even close. I'm still right in the thick of it, every single day. I’m still dealing with all these impossible deadlines they keep throwing at me—like, they need this tax form by Tuesday, or that proof of income by Thursday, and if I miss it by an hour, they threaten to just lock the doors. And the calls... I'm still dealing with the constant phone calls. It's always some different person from the bank's loss mitigation department, and they always want a different piece of paper that I swear I already faxed them three weeks ago. It's just maddening. 

So, you know, this whole state I'm in, it hasn't continued past the end of the problem, because there hasn't been an end yet. The problem is still happening right now. There hasn't been any sort of finish line for my brain to even try and recover from, you know what I mean? It's like... you can't heal a burn while your hand is still pressed flat against the hot exhaust manifold. And my hand is definitely still on the manifold. If it was over, if it was all fixed and in the rearview mirror, I know I'd be fine. I'd go back to just being me, turning wrenches and going home to a house that's actually mine. But right now, with the deadlines still looming and the phone still ringing... it's just not over, so the panic isn't over either.
Do you think your anxiety would be present even if you weren't constantly thinking about your financial and work situation?

No, honestly, I really don't. Because... well, the thing is, I can't even separate the two right now to even test that theory. I don't have a single minute in my day where I'm not thinking about the house or the shop. 

It's like... you know when you've got a bad wheel bearing on a rig, and you're driving down the highway, and there's that constant, low-grade hum? You turn up the radio, you roll down the window, you try to talk over it, but that hum is always there, vibrating right up through the floorboards into your boots. That's exactly what my brain is doing right now. I'll go home, heat up some dinner, and try to watch TV—maybe put on some old rerun or something just to shut my mind off for twenty minutes—and I just can't do it. My mind just drifts right back to, "Did I sign that second page of the affidavit?" or "Is Dave gonna cut my hours again next week?" 

And the second that thought pops into my head, the panic is right there riding shotgun with it. My chest gets tight, my stomach drops, and I'm right back in it. But if you could somehow magically reach into my head and just pluck those specific thoughts out? No, I wouldn't be anxious at all. I really don't think I would be. 

Because before all this started, I was the most laid-back person you'd ever meet. I've been doing this a long time, and I always had a strict rule—I'd leave the shop, scrub the grease off my hands with the pumice soap, and that was it. Work stayed at work, home was home, and my mind was quiet. I never had this kind of buzzing in my chest before. Now it's just all bleeding together in this big, messy puddle of stress. So, no, the anxiety is completely, one hundred percent attached to the thoughts about the bank and my job. If I wasn't thinking about them... well, I guess I wouldn't be having this problem at all. But the reality is I just can't stop thinking about them, no matter what I try to do to distract myself.
Do you think you would be anxious about other things in your life if the foreclosure and work issues were resolved?

No, I really don't. I mean... what else is there to even worry about, really? Because before the bank started sending those letters and things went sideways at the shop, my life was just... it was simple. And I liked it that way. I'm a pretty straightforward person, you know? I go to work, I turn my hours, I come home, maybe grill a steak on the back patio or tinker with my old Chevy in the driveway. There's no... there's no big drama in my life outside of this mess. 

I've just never been a worrier. Like, my sister, for example, she'll call me up absolutely frantic because she thinks the cashier at the grocery store gave her a dirty look, or because she's convinced it's going to rain on some weekend trip she planned three months from now. She can spin herself up over absolutely nothing. But me? I've always been the practical one. If a serpentine belt is squeaking, you replace the belt. If the roof leaks, you get up there with some tar and patch it. You fix what's in front of you and you don't sweat the rest. 

So if you take away the threat of losing my home, and you take away Dave breathing down my neck and making me feel like my job is on the line every single day... there's just nothing else waiting in the wings to jump out and scare me. It's just a blank slate. Those two things—the foreclosure and the shop—that's the whole engine right there. If you fix those two cylinders, the whole thing runs smooth again. I really, truly believe that. I just don't have anything else going on that would ever make me feel like this.
Do you think your anxiety would persist even after your financial and work situation has been completely resolved and you are no longer experiencing any stress from those areas?

Honestly, doc, like I was saying a minute ago... no. I really don't think it would stick around at all. I know we kind of just touched on this, but it’s just the absolute truth—the only reason I'm still feeling like this is because the foreclosure process still isn't resolved. Not even a little bit. I am still, right this very second, dealing with all the impossible deadlines and the constant phone calls. 

It’s not like the bank shook my hand, fixed my mortgage, and I’m just sitting here months later still sweating and shaking for no reason. No, this whole panic... it hasn't continued past the end of the problem, because we haven't even reached the end of the problem yet! The problem is still sitting right there on my kitchen counter in a stack of manila envelopes. Just yesterday, I got another letter—certified mail, too, so you have to actually sign for it, which just makes your stomach drop the second you see the mail carrier walking up the driveway with that little green slip. And it's always just more deadlines. They want this statement, they want that affidavit. 

And the calls, my god, the calls. I'll be under a rig at the shop, literally up to my elbows in grease and hydraulic fluid, trying to drop a heavy transmission, and my phone starts buzzing in my pocket. I don't even have to look at the screen anymore to know it's the bank's loss mitigation department calling to ask me the exact same questions they asked me on Tuesday. So, because all of that is still actively happening, I'm still actively a wreck. 

If it were completely resolved—like, if the bank sent a letter saying 'modification approved' and Dave finally backed off at work and let me just turn my wrenches in peace—I know I’d be fine. It would be exactly like... well, like when you finally track down a bad electrical short in a wiring harness. You know how frustrating that is? You're chasing ghosts, the check engine light keeps coming on, the engine is misfiring, and it drives you crazy. But the second you finally find that one frayed wire, splice it, tape it up, and clear the computer codes... the dashboard light stays off. The problem is gone. The truck runs fine again. 

That's exactly how my brain would be. Once this mess with the house and the shop is actually fixed, the warning lights in my head are going to shut off. I know they will. But right now, the wire is still sparking, you know? The stress is still completely active, so my brain is still throwing codes.

Do you think your anxiety would decrease if you were able to find a way to cope with or resolve the stressors related to your financial and work situation, without actually changing your circumstances?

I... I don't really know how to answer that, doc, because... well, what does that even look like? Coping without actually changing the circumstances? I'm not sure I even understand how that's possible. 

It’s like... okay, say a guy brings a Peterbilt into my bay, right? And it’s got a cracked engine block. Oil is leaking everywhere, coolant is mixing where it shouldn't be, the whole thing is an absolute disaster just waiting to seize up completely on the interstate. You can’t just... sit in the cab, turn on some relaxing music, and 'cope' with the cracked block. You can’t just change your mindset about the engine block. It’s still cracked! It’s still going to blow! No amount of positive thinking is going to weld that cast iron back together. 

That’s exactly how I feel about this whole mess. My sister, actually, she was telling me just the other day that I should try meditation. Or deep breathing exercises, or drinking chamomile tea before bed, or whatever it is people do. And I’m just sitting there listening to her, thinking, "How on earth is breathing in through my nose and out through my mouth going to stop the sheriff from putting a padlock on my front door?" It doesn't change a single thing. The bank still wants their money, and Dave is still going to be standing over my shoulder tomorrow morning complaining about my turnaround times on the brake jobs. 

So, I don't know. I really don't. Maybe there are people out there who can just zen their way through losing everything they’ve worked for over the last twenty years, but I’m just not wired like that. I'm a mechanic. If there’s a failure in the system, I need to fix the failure. I can’t just learn to live with the warning lights flashing in my face twenty-four hours a day. Unless the actual problems go away, I don't see how any amount of... of coping skills or whatever is going to make my chest stop feeling like it’s caught in a vice grip. I just don't have any idea how that would even work.
Do you think you would ever worry about things to the point of feeling anxious even if you didn't have any major stressors in your life?

Doc, I feel like we're kind of going in circles here, because... well, no. I really, truly wouldn't. Like I was saying a few minutes ago, if there's no major stressor—if the engine isn't actively on fire—I'm not going to sit around sweating about whether it *might* catch fire someday. That's just not who I am. 

I've got 47 years of evidence proving I don't do that. Back before all this mess started, before Dave started breathing down my neck at the shop and the bank started hounding me, my days were just... they were peaceful. I'd go to the depot, do my shift—usually working on the big earthmovers, the Caterpillars, you know, the really heavy equipment that actually takes some muscle and brainpower to keep running. I'd do my job, wash the grease off my hands with that gritty orange pumice soap, and come home. And once I was home, my brain was completely off the clock. 

I wasn't pacing the floors wondering if the water heater was going to break, or if the grocery store was going to run out of my favorite coffee, or what somebody meant when they said hello to me weird. I'd just sit on the porch, maybe have a beer, watch the neighbor's dog chase squirrels, and that was it. My mind was quiet. I don't have this... this built-in need to find things to panic about. 

I really think some people are just born with their idle set too high, you know? Like my sister, like I mentioned. Her brain is just constantly revving, constantly looking for a problem to latch onto even when everything is perfectly fine. But my idle has always been set perfectly low. If there's nothing broken, I don't go looking for something to fix. So no, if you take away the actual, real-life disasters happening to me right now, I wouldn't be worrying to the point of feeling like this. I just wouldn't. I'd go right back to being the exact same person I was before the mail carrier started bringing me certified letters.
Do you think you would be anxious about things other than your financial and work situation if you were no longer preoccupied with those issues?

I mean, doc, I really feel like I’m beating a dead horse here, but no. Absolutely not. If you take away the bank threatening to take my home, and you take away Dave making my life a living hell at the shop... what else is there for me to even sweat over? Normal life stuff? That stuff has never bothered me. Never. 

Like, okay, just to give you an example... a couple of years ago, way before any of this current mess started, my water heater completely rusted out. Just gave up the ghost. The bottom dropped right out of it while I was at work, and it flooded the entire utility room. Messed up the drywall, soaked a bunch of boxes of old clothes I had stored in there, just a huge, soggy disaster. Now, someone else—like my sister, who I was just talking about—she would have had a total meltdown. She’d be crying about black mold, calling three different emergency plumbers in an absolute panic, hyperventilating about the foundation rotting away. 

But me? I came home, saw the water, and I just... dealt with it. I shut off the main valve, grabbed the shop vac, spent three hours sucking up dirty water, and then the next morning I drove my truck down to the hardware store, bought a new 50-gallon tank and some PEX tubing, and I swapped it out myself. Was it annoying? Sure, nobody wants to spend their Saturday doing plumbing. Did it cost me a few hundred bucks I didn't want to spend? Yeah. But did my chest get tight? Did I lose sleep over it? Was I shaking and sweating and feeling like the world was ending? No. Not even for a second. Because it was just a normal problem, and normal problems have normal fixes. 

So if this whole situation with the mortgage and the shop gets resolved, I'm not going to suddenly start having... I don't know, freak-outs about the price of eggs, or whether it's going to rain on my day off, or if my truck needs new brake pads. I just deal with normal things normally. It’s only this... this massive, impossible, life-ruining mountain of garbage hanging over my head that has me spun out like this. If you take those specific things away, there is absolutely nothing else in my life that would make me feel this way. I just don't have that kind of personality. I fix what's broken, I wash my hands, and I move on.
